snippet.textDisplay:
"Industrialists created a system where the majority of people live in poverty"
Industrialization did not create the original human condition of poverty. Poverty was historically normal. The unusual development is mass affluence. The World Bank estimates that the number of people in extreme poverty worldwide fell from roughly 2.3 billion in 1990 to 831 million in 2025, despite major world population growth. Much of that economic growth came from the introduction of more free market policies across the globe.

snippet.textDisplay:
"There's not enough government funding for all of us to be housed."

Money is not housing. The actual scarce resources are land, structures, construction labor, materials, financing, and permission to build. Government can redistribute purchasing power, but it cannot make those real resources cease to be scarce. The correction question is, "why are high prices not inducing enough additional housing construction?" If density limits, permitting, zoning, parking requirements, building restrictions, and other barriers prevent supply from responding, simply appropriating more money treats the price symptom without removing the underlying scarcity.

snippet.textDisplay:
"80% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck."

This is just not factually true. Here's what the data looks like:

In 2025:

63 percent could cover a $400 emergency using cash or its equivalent
70 percent could cover at least a $500 expense using savings
55 percent had three months of emergency savings
30 percent could not cover three months of expenses even using borrowing, asset sales, or other savings
only 12 percent said they could not cover a $400 emergency by any method

That's according to the federal reserve. implying nearly four-fifths of Americans are one missed paycheck from homelessness greatly exaggerates what the data show.

snippet.textDisplay:
"Most wealth is held by White people, therefore Black Americans are being exploited."

There is no reason to expect racial groups with different histories and characteristics to produce identical statistical outcomes even in the complete absence of discrimination.

So a disparity cannot simply be converted into:

difference = discrimination = exploitation.

Specific discrimination requires specific evidence.

Likewise, another person's wealth is not proof that corresponding wealth was taken from someone else. Wealth can be created when businesses, property, skills, or capital become more valuable.

It’s so easy to say there’s a way when you’re a millionaire or even when you make high to figures salary, you couldn’t possibly imagine the hoops that people like I’ve, working an $11 an hour job and small town, has to jump through to even get my bills paid on time and I am a woman in my 30s without children. I could only imagine if I did have children and then tagging along a baby daddy who probably isn’t in the picture or only making things worse very rarely do you have a spouse that still in your corner helping you. It’s so easy to say that you have opportunity when you are a millionaire you don’t know what it’s like to have to look for a resources all the freaking time on your phone. You’re spending so much time on your phone looking for resources or signing up for this waitlist in hopes of getting cheap housing or you know food stamps or you know whatever you’re sitting might be holding some kind of nonprofit you know this or that it’s it’s not easy you know and I think it has to do also with what you’re born into if you were born into a household of middle to lower Class people you will probably end up especially in this economy low class if not, you’re a paycheck away from becoming homeless so many people have become homeless versus being a child who grew up in a home that had major money and his family that was always happy because there was nothing to complain about I mean, of course everybody has issues. I’m not saying that but a household that’s on a low spectrum versus household that makes six figures you’re gonna have happier people living in that home than you would in a home that is totally wrapped in stress and chaos and you know not knowing where your next meal is going to be. You cannot tell me that being poor is a choice that is an absolutely asinine statement.

snippet.textDisplay:
This is where we have to define "comfortable" because with the advancement of technology and the over-stimulation of Social Media and the increasing desire for convenience over necessity, people make it seem like living "comfortably" should be synonymous with living "luxuriously" and those things need to be kept distinct from each other. 

An individual working an entry-level full-time job should be able to afford the following: rent for a 1BR apartment, utilities (including standard internet), groceries, and clothes (able to get some new drip either during their birthday or the holidays) for themselves, while still having enough money to float an emergency. Anything beyond that would be elevating from living comfortably to living luxuriously, and luxury isn't entry-level living/comfort.  

Living comfortably does NOT necessitate: affording rent, utilities, groceries, car payment (or two), all the streaming platforms, gaming consoles, high end smart phones, tablets, drones, designer clothes, Jordans and what have you. These are luxuries, not necessities, and sometimes people attempt to live above their means because they desire a degree of comfort and convenience beyond what they can afford and don't want to hustle the extra to afford it, yet still expect it. And there are people who will forgo certain things for others, for example they'll downsize to a studio apartment with a smaller bathroom and kitchenette so they can have that fancy phone and afford a streaming service or 3. 

So yeah, still have to be reasonable and realistic about what one defines as "living comfortably". And I say this as someone who's worked on building himself up to afford some level of luxury, but still helps out friends, family and strangers in need when the opportunities to help present themselves.

snippet.textDisplay:
Yo…..

I have been unhoused for two years as a trans individual in a cold hearthed city and I chose not to cope with drugs and go to the gym instead. I was training and showering in a private gym alongside CEO. I never chose victim mentality or scarcity mindset in spite of the situations and took those hardships as stepping stones. I’m now in SRO and am working and recording an album and is actively working on my spiritual life, doing meditation every day. This place, this skid row is far from perfect but it is a lesson to enrich my mind and heart. It’s not the end goal. If you chose in your mind that you have perspectives, you gonna find proofs around.

I broke free from my parents patterns with alcohol and I’m the only one in my family who took the leap of faith to switch from the East Coast from the West Coast. To me that’s a start.

I do believe the words we chose are important and the identity we embody is in our hands. I was showering every day and dressing classy, passing for a high class person downtown while I was sleeping on a mat same day around mices and people with drug addiction. I do believe scarcity mindset is a choice. Everything is mind. You chose your POV.

To me, I am abundant and always been in many many ways.

snippet.textDisplay: Of course is not a conscious choice, no one wants to be homeless. It's a collection of unconscious decisions that get you to the point. Obviously I don't have the time to sit down with somebody and navigate through every single choice they've made in their life, But I can guarantee you, They could have made better ones, Even I could have made better ones and maybe I would be in a better spot. At the end of the day, you cannot afford to be a victim. You can't afford to be a reactive person. You have to be proactive to get out of poverty. And for everyone that looks in different ways, but at the end of the day, if you really feel like you don't have any other choice, anyone can join the military. No matter who you are, you can walk into a recruiting station for any of the four branches and join. The only excuse you might have is a medical condition or having a kid. And if you do have a kid, the only thing you need to figure out is who's going to take care of the kid for three months while you're at basic. I promise you there are programs and resources that will help you take care of your kid for three months So that you can join the military . Of course, the military doesn't pay super well, but you are guaranteed to have housing. You have a guaranteed paycheck every two weeks. And the longer you stay, the more money you make. So no, These are all excuses to be a victim. Some of this stuff is valid. Bad things do happen. Racism is a thing. Some people don't get the same opportunity as others, but there is a path forward, no matter who you are. No, I'm not saying it's easy. I'm not saying that getting out of poverty is as simple as joining the military. I'm just saying that the options are there, and it's up to you to take the step.

"Being poor is a choice"? This is not true in principle. Nature's normal behavior is to balance charge and conservation of energy. Money IS the potential energy stored from actual energy in terms of whatever physical property is claimed as one's OWN. 'Ownership" is an artificial construct given animals normally have restrictions to their present natural capacity to stand their territorial grounds. So OWNERSHIP itself is a PRIVILEGE that the whole of society merely created because we have managed to go beyond our capacity to use TOOLS as weapons. 

If you are born into poverty, you lack the recommendations from family who could give you the little things that add essential value to one's capacity to succeed. So such poverty originating people require ENTRY LEVEL jobs that can enable them to do so. But these low-level entry level jobs disfavor them because they are not the compassionate middle class union worker whose relatives get first pick or if quotas are tried, they exclude those who have been born here,  especially those who do not align themselves with 'ethnic' groups or religion. Thus the ones who DO hire tend to be these very millionaire OWNERS of industries that hire the desperate with the LEAST economic incentive .....and if they especially LOCK those people into their employ.

Furthermore, the bar for entry level jobs ends up preferring the teenagers of the wealthier classes. But because the norm for wealthier classes is to allow their youth to live at home 'free', the poor have to accept the WAY those entry level jobs are designed to favor things like PART TIME labor, ....especially where politicians find that sponsoring the exploiting capitalists to get tax benefits and exceptions of normal employers rights reserved for those with full time jobs. 

Physics would tell us that energy is conserved. Money as a form of artificial energy cheats when it allows one to make MORE than another. The mere fact that you can 'save' a debt as an I-owe-you is itself artificial construct that favors EXPONENTIAL wealth creation in an amplification of imbalance. So ....

...For one person among three to be even slightly better off REQUIRES a loss of that distributed value as 'energy' among the other two. This 'distribution' is hard for one to not notice. A poor person born into it also cannot afford to FAIL even ONCE most often. But to better off people, they CAN afford to fail by the various supports they have including the community class level norms most of them take advantage of as though EVERYONE has such normal background. That mere fact to be able to fail is an example of how UNFAIR the system is against the poor .....while RELYING on people to be IN DEBT for another to have that in terms of monetary value.

snippet.textDisplay:
Oof - Kate missed the plot when she answered the second question. The difference is the intentionality. “Slavery” may have ended “300 years ago,” but the Pullman Porters lasted until 1968. Chicago experienced high volumes of “white flight,” a practice meant to tank property values for black residents, in the 1980s and then they also introduced drugs into their abandoned neighborhoods. The Crown Act, which prohibits discrimination by HAIR TEXTURE (I.e., deeming African-descent hair as automatically unprofessional) was created in 2019 and is still only in 27 states. Milagro is passionate to the point of disagreeableness, that’s clear. He would EXCEL as a professor though! That said, to his credit, there’s data that show some structures are strategically in place to keep the poor and several minority groups down. Psychologically or otherwise. You can still work hard, but you can’t not acknowledge there’s legitimate and real systems out there that benefit some (e.g., we’re in the same fraternity so I’ll help you) and exclude others (e.g., you have a criminal record so now you can’t work here because you failed a background check). It’s like the curve “someone has to fail to benefit the rest.”

Last example: Section 8 housing. I knew someone (white, likely high-functioning autistic) who made 25 cents more/hr and his rent went up $200. He chose to not take a promotion because it put him in a worse spot overall. The hurdle to cross that invisible chasm is wider than the millionaires see from their vantage point. No one can do it alone.

snippet.textDisplay: As someone who grew up really poor, being poor is a choice could be reframed as “Lack of discipline supersedes wanting to not be poor”. Many times where there was no money came from a bad choice or selfish decision made by parents rather than just a system keeping them from getting above it. Hence why the guy who pointed to his head and saying “sometimes people lose here first” had a point when it came down to people not having the control and discipline. There are plenty of folks who will go without eating and suffer through the storm, paycheck through paycheck until they have enough to do something different with their lives. Sometimes the hardships of being broke or barely making money can cause folk to get into distracting themselves from it by addictions, shopping addictions, going out more than they should. The person who won’t get a job because they don’t have a car vs the ones who will get a job no matter the distance and catch the bus and wake up really early just to get there on time. Folks leaving their house an hour or 2 later to get to the same job while ones who are riding the bus were up hours before. A discipline. It is not that I am trying to say its a complete choice, but its like sometimes the choices you make signal the choice you didn’t exclusively made but relatively the same. Choosing to ride with your headlights off at night is nearly the same as choosing to get into an accident.

snippet.textDisplay:
This conversation was particularly frustrating because many of the debaters lacked context, nuance, and, above all, compassion. For instance, when Kate completely dismissed the historical context of American slavery and the ongoing systemic injustices that have negatively impacted African Americans and other people of color, she made a casual comparison to slavery in Russia, stating, "Oh, that was a long time ago." This perspective grossly invalidates the lasting effects on entire populations.

Additionally, there was a lot of commentary regarding "choices." While I don't disagree that some decisions can impact one's trajectory in life, I do not believe that everyone is perceived the same based on their choices, and as a result, not everyone is punished or rewarded the same way. Some wealthy individuals in the discussion may not acknowledge how privilege, environment, and dysfunctional social systems contribute to disproportionate outcomes for certain people. There are circumstances that many of them would never experience because of who they are.

Ultimately, we all need to be kind. When we are fortunate enough to have more opportunities or resources, we should look to support those who are vulnerable.

snippet.textDisplay:
The bandana guy is so annoying with his victim mentality. I am a black woman and I truly believe that poverty is for many people a choice. Everybody have challenges, goes through obstacles. The difference between someone with a fixed/poverty mindset and growth mindset is that people with a growth mindset see solutions, opportunities, chances, possibilities. People with a poverty/fixed mindset don't want to see those things, they see only problems, no solutions. They choose to stay stuck where they are, refuse to move forward to make their life better, believe that they are a victim and blaming other people for their problems. 

There are so many ways to make more money by: getting a better job, monetize your passion, learn a new skill & master it and monetize it, and the one you make most money with is: start a business and solve problems for rich people who need your services or products. 

I had a poverty mindset and victim mentality. I blamed others for the mistakes I made and my circumstances. The last few years I shifted that and I hold myself accountable for my choices and actions. I don't see myself as a victim of my circumstances anymore. I decided that I want to make more money and started my own business, I work with great clients and have 5 figure months. It's all a choices and it's starts with changing your mindset and rewriting your story, so you can shift your identity and become empowered to see whatever happened in your past was a lesson, an experience that helped you to become who you are today. You are not meant to stay stuck, but become a more empowered version of yourself.

snippet.textDisplay: Being poor isn’t simply a choice. Yes, upward mobility is possible in America — but possibility ≠ access. When people grow up without financial literacy, stability, representation, or fully funded schools, they’re operating in survival mode. You can’t invest or plan long-term when basic needs aren’t met. Add in low wages, time poverty, and historical destruction of Black wealth (Black Wall Street, OTR, redlining), and the “choice” argument ignores reality. People can make it out — but poverty persists largely because of knowledge gaps, environment, and systemic barriers, not laziness.

snippet.textDisplay:
The problem with a victim mentality is that it avoids solutions because solutions require accountability. When someone claims you cannot participate in a conversation because of your race, gender, age, or background, they are shutting down any chance of constructive dialogue. The same dynamic appears in discussions about childbirth, firearms, immigration, and many other issues.

Not owning a gun does not invalidate someone’s opinion. It simply means they bring a different perspective. Likewise, being an immigrant can provide valuable insight into immigration, but it can also limit awareness of how policies affect others in different ways. Perspective adds context, but it should not be used as a weapon to silence opposing views.

When you encounter someone who consistently dismisses disagreement, assigns malicious intent to conversations meant to be challenging but constructive, or frames themselves as a professional victim, it is often best not to engage. Unfortunately, some individuals claim to speak for an entire community while, in reality, making that community appear unreasonable or intolerant.

Meaningful discussion becomes impossible when someone believes they already understand everything while simultaneously portraying themselves as powerless. The irony is that this mindset undermines the very progress it claims to seek.

The same dynamic appears in discussions about childbirth, firearms, immigration, and many other issues.

Not owning a gun does not invalidate someone’s opinion. It simply means they bring a different perspective. Likewise, being an immigrant can provide valuable insight into immigration, but it can also limit awareness of how policies affect others in different ways. Perspective adds context, but it should not be used as a weapon to silence opposing views.

When you encounter someone who consistently dismisses disagreement, assigns malicious intent to conversations meant to be challenging but constructive, or frames themselves as a professional victim, it is often best not to engage. Unfortunately, some individuals claim to speak for an entire community while, in reality, making that community appear unreasonable or intolerant.

Meaningful discussion becomes impossible when someone believes they already understand everything while simultaneously portraying themselves as powerless. The irony is that this mindset undermines the very progress it claims to seek.

snippet.textDisplay:
Poverty isn’t a choice. If it were, we wouldn’t see wealth line up almost exactly with the historical advantages people are born into. In the U.S., about 76% of millionaires are White, while Black and Hispanic communities remain under-represented—not because of ‘bad choices,’ but because of generations of unequal access to education, housing, credit, and inherited wealth. People don’t choose their parents, their ZIP code, their school quality, or whether they face discrimination. The starting line simply is not the same for everyone.

And homelessness proves it even more. Dallas just showed what happens when a city stops judging people and actually acts. The Austin Street Center and other partners got tired of watching homelessness grow, so instead of blaming individuals, they tackled the systemic causes. They went into the community, did real outreach, zone by zone, and placed people into real housing—not shelters, not temporary fixes, but homes. The program is working, and there are videos on YouTube documenting how effective it’s been.

This is what happens when we treat homelessness as a systemic failure, not a personal flaw. Poverty and homelessness don’t disappear by telling people to ‘choose better.’ They disappear when we build systems that give people real opportunities, safety, and stability.

snippet.textDisplay:
The millionaire guy asked, “Do you think you can be exceptional?” as if that somehow proves a point. But that’s actually the whole problem. It doesn’t matter whether someone can be exceptional or not. A person shouldn’t have to be a one-percenter to deserve food in their stomach, a roof over their head, or basic dignity.
A humane society doesn’t reserve survival for the gifted few.
Thriving shouldn’t be a prize for the exceptional. It should be a guarantee for everyone, including the “average,” the struggling, and the people who will never be extraordinary by capitalist standards.
That’s the difference they never seem to understand.

Another part of the problem is how deeply individualistic our society has become. We’ve lost any sense of “I am my brother’s keeper.” Everything is framed as me and mine, and if the person next door is starving, people shrug because it’s “not their problem.”
But a healthy society isn’t built on everyone fending for themselves. It’s built on community, responsibility, and recognizing that our well being is tied together.
We thrive when we care about each other, not when we treat survival like a solo competition.

snippet.textDisplay: I live a relatively stable middle class life with a family and a house and two cars and a career and even I'm not blind that there are people who through no fault of their own were born into a system where reaching economic stability let alone accumulating wealth is basically impossible.  My eyes basically rolled every time the millionaires talked about how easy it is for everyone to become successful.  The woman from Russia especially rubbed me the wrong way talking about how people can just choose not to be poor, especially when she said they should just buy a bus ticket to West Virginia as if people have the money and resources to relocate and have a house waiting for them on the other side of the country. While true communism, Marxist-Leninist,  is based on the principles of the social-economic norm of being able to truly give equal access and opportunities to everyone. Milagro and Jack know what it means too struggle because of the societal imbalances in this world, they portray that in their answers and messages.

I am not saying communism is the solution for world happiness, but capitalism is by it self very pro-violence (if it is social, economic or physical but most often they all play a role together).

P.s. I am not saying the millionaires are purposefully causing social violence, I think our societal system has made them violent without their knowledge... Indoctrination is a historical pattern, would be naive to assume it doesn`t exist in the capitalistic west.

snippet.textDisplay:
Unhoused didn't fall below my expectations for ability to articulate intelligent thought. Millionaires on the other hand really helped me reinforce the wisdom that suggests wealth (at the very least at the million benchmark) isn't synonymous with the same/previous factor.

A lot of people come into money, but don't understand all the factors that allowed for them to get there. And of the ones that do, there's another significant portion of them that struggle to see certain demographics of their fellow countrymen as being more like the disadvantaged in certain foreign countries than like them. There are Americans that have more in common with the average Syrian or perhaps Ukrainian or perhaps Palestinian than they do with someone living an hour or two or three away from where they park or camp/pitch —financially and "opportunity" wise. It's hard to really quantify the lottery of life.


It doesn't benefit a rich person to do the math of, demographics x & y have a genetic disposition to fall into drug abuse due to their parents' decisions, and so of x & y who end up in car accidents or workplace accidents or sports injuries and get given certain drug medications in the hospital —they are disproportionately going to fall victim to addiction to drugs provided by hospitals. Was being born in demo x & y, or being in a vehicle while someone else was careless or intoxicated, or playing competitive sports a choice for poverty? Surely not. Surely some people make routinely bad decisions, but I suspect some of the laziest people have jobs and just find ways to manipulate others into sustaining them rather than choosing poverty. Anyone who's tasted poverty of a certain type understands that most healthy people never choose that.

It's so intellectually unsatisfying for rich people to have strong opinions while under informed. Knowing a lot about your craft doesn't make you economically wise, and economists are notoriously known for their odd economic and financial opinions. A millionaire should be that much more humble imo

And maybe I'm dead wrong
And if I am, I'm super sorry

snippet.textDisplay: People who say the Black guy is a "victim" aren't really listening to him. I think he makes some great points on how history and the current system impact people and different communities. It's not as easy as "pulling yourself up by your bootstraps." A lot of people who have faced incredible violence and oppression (that most of us can't even wrap our heads around) live with generations of trauma that are unknowingly passed down. Without community support, reparations, or truthful education, how do people expect communities to live like the past never happened? I work in the field of education in a pretty liberal place, and kids STILL do not learn about the Reconstruction Era, the United States' involvement in Civil Wars in Central America and Africa (which has led to mass migration to Western countries), or the extent of slavery. Did you know that New York almost joined the Confederacy to maintain their extensive system of slavery? Did you know that New York had the 2nd biggest slavery auction in the country? It's crazy to me that people blame individuals for not seizing opportunities, but the current system we have in place does not make it easy for people to do that. Just my 2 cents. I highly recommend Clint Smith's book "How the Word is Passed." Also, can someone please explain to me why there is such a large population of homeless veterans??? Those people LITERALLY pulled themselves by their bootstraps and still do not have access to basic amenities.

snippet.textDisplay: As a Black African-American male, I want to address a concern I have regarding perceptions within the Black community. It often seems that many African-Americans adopt a victim mentality, believing that their circumstances are solely due to their race. However, I believe that poverty is, in many ways, a choice. I own three different companies, and my name is not publicly associated with any of them. People are often unaware of my race or background. What matters is the quality of the product or service and how effectively it is marketed. Success is achievable for anyone, regardless of race. If you feel that your race is holding you back, there are ways to overcome those barriers. You have the power to create the life you desire, and no one can stop you but yourself. Instead of focusing on fame or recognition, consider that being unknown can actually be an advantage. It allows you to operate without the pressure of public scrutiny and gives you the freedom to innovate. I encourage all to shift their mindset. Embrace the opportunities available to you, work hard, and prioritize personal growth over societal labels. Your potential is not defined by your race but by your determination and resilience.

snippet.textDisplay:
Video berjudul "Is Being Poor a Choice? Unhoused vs Millionaires | Middle Ground" mempertemukan dua kelompok dengan latar belakang ekonomi yang sangat berbeda, yaitu tunawisma dan jutawan. Mereka mendiskusikan berbagai topik kontroversial seputar kemiskinan dan tunawisma untuk mencari titik tengah dan memahami sudut pandang satu sama lain.
Berikut adalah penjelasan terstruktur dari topik-topik utama yang dibahas dalam video:
 * "Menjadi miskin adalah pilihan." [00:24]
   * Sisi Jutawan: Umumnya setuju, berpendapat bahwa setiap orang memiliki waktu yang sama dalam sehari dan cara memanfaatkannya menentukan nasib. Mereka juga menyoroti banyaknya peluang di era modern, seperti teknologi.
   * Sisi Tunawisma: Sangat tidak setuju, menjelaskan bahwa banyak faktor di luar kendali yang menyebabkan kemiskinan, seperti trauma, diskriminasi rasial, dan kurangnya kesempatan.
 * "Kapitalisme menciptakan tunawisma." [14:43]
   * Sisi Tunawisma: Berpendapat bahwa kapitalisme adalah sistem eksploitatif yang membuat orang kaya semakin kaya dan orang miskin semakin miskin, tanpa insentif untuk membantu tunawisma.
   * Sisi Jutawan: Membedakan antara kapitalisme murni dan "cronyism," meyakini bahwa kapitalisme adalah sistem yang indah dan telah menciptakan banyak peluang.
 * "Perkemahan tunawisma bisa berbahaya dan harus dibersihkan." [23:21]
   * Sisi Jutawan: Setuju, berdasarkan pengalaman pribadi melihat penggunaan narkoba dan kekerasan. Mereka juga menganggap perkemahan tidak sedap dipandang.
   * Sisi Tunawisma: Berpendapat bahwa perkemahan adalah satu-satunya pilihan karena kurangnya dukungan pemerintah dan fasilitas. Mereka merasa perkemahan memberikan rasa komunitas.
 * "Sistem ini direkayasa untuk membuat orang kaya tetap kaya dan orang miskin tetap miskin." [35:57]
   * Sisi Tunawisma: Sangat setuju, menyoroti kebijakan pemerintah yang menguntungkan orang kaya dan statistik yang menunjukkan seseorang cenderung tetap berada di kelas sosial tempat mereka dilahirkan.
   * Sisi Jutawan: Mengakui sistem memang "direkayasa" sampai batas tertentu, tetapi tidak percaya bahwa sistem ini mencegah siapa pun untuk berhasil.
 * "Orang kaya memiliki kewajiban untuk mengatasi tunawisma." [44:39]
   * Kedua Sisi: Setuju bahwa orang kaya memiliki tanggung jawab untuk membantu, baik melalui uang, pendidikan, atau reformasi. Di akhir video, salah satu jutawan bahkan memberikan voucher hotel kepada para tunawisma sebagai wujud empati. [47:22]
Video ini menyimpulkan bahwa tidak ada jawaban tunggal untuk masalah yang kompleks ini. Namun, melalui dialog, video menunjukkan bagaimana empati dapat menjembatani perbedaan antara kedua kelompok.

snippet.textDisplay:
Having a real conversation with someone who is poor when you’re a dollar millionaire is almost impossible. The gap isn’t just financial; it’s mental. Poor people always have reasons for their situation. They believe them, defend them, and you can see it in their eyes and their energy. The wealthy are no different. Truly rich people have their reasons, excuses, and narratives about why they are rich, and they hold them just as passionately.

But most people, even those considered “rich,” aren’t truly wealthy. If you have to wake up every morning just to keep your life running - pay the bills, put food on the table, keep a roof over your head; you are not rich. True wealth is when your life can sustain itself without constant effort.

The biggest difference between the "rich" and the "poor" isn’t money; it’s mindset! Consumerism traps the majority. I’ve seen poor people live lifestyles that many wealthy people can’t afford simply because they spend more than they earn without a meaningful return. This isn’t random; it’s systemic. Capitalism thrives on consumers, and society benefits when people remain uneducated and dependent. Like most "rich" people, I rely on the poor to work, spend, to keep the economy running in order for my net-worth to double/triple/quadruple.

The truly wealthy live differently; MOST of us leverage debt and assets, we delay gratification, and quietly build independence. Most people chase comfort and validation today, while I keep trying and failing at everything; It’s not glamorous, it gets lonely and is not fashionable to the average person. You will lose friends in most cases, and society may reject you. You will have to sacrifice short-term pleasures to secure long-term freedom without any guarantee at times.

But make no mistake: the payoff is unimaginable. True wealth isn’t measured in liquid money, it’s measured in control over your life, your time, and your future. Most people will never achieve it because they aren’t wired for it. And that’s why the gap between the rich and poor will always exist.

Am I rich? Not according to me.

snippet.textDisplay:
"Trauma is subjective" is a serious misunderstanding of the science. Yes, two people can go through the same experience and incur different amounts of trauma. That's because trauma is based on how unsafe we feel in the moment, not how severe the event is. 

This doesn't mean the one who incurs more trauma is weaker or choosing to have a victim attitude - their brain was physiologically more impacted by the event! Not a choice and not something within the person's control.

snippet.textDisplay:
They choose to do things that lead them to poverty but no one says "I want to be poor" and then become poor.
Very often, these people are unaware of the negative repercussions their choices, or had been forced or pressured into making those choices.
And, from another way to look at it, what is the point of looking at someone with addiction, debt, or someone that doesn't spend their money well and telling them "this is your fault, you deserve this, you chose this"? It seems unproductive to say that. It doesn't make sense, there is no benefit for anyone there.

edit: I think the statement "being poor is a choice" has only been created for sensationalism, for the market where views, engagement, and discussion are the profit. It's very broad. It can mean so many things and it seeks to trigger the people who are going to take that personally. It's almost inevitable that when you share your opinion using that statement as a baseline that it's going to come out as vague and that the solution you are looking for won't be correctly represented.

snippet.textDisplay:
Are we talking about poverty or just a general "poor"? I would argue that poor can just mean not rich. Even if you're middle class you're probably struggling or one paycheck away from losing your home or being kicked out of your rented home. Most people are prisoners of the system/economy. Everyone can't be rich in a fiat currency system. If everyone is rich then nobody is rich. Money is devalued. A fiat currency system is based off of debt and inflation. I'm not even specifically talking about capitalism which is based off of exploitation and hierarchy, but capitalism is not even close to being the "best" system. There are going to be flaws in every system, but I think an actual representation of socialism would be better for workers. I'm just talking about owning the means of production and not all of these other inaccurate definitions of socialism. People always also want to compare capitalism with communism and I think it's a false equivalency. I think it's more accurate to compare fascism with communism.

Capitalism isn't even capitalism today. There is intervention from the state and corporations. What we have today that people think is capitalism is closer to oligarchy or even neo-fascism. Those who own capital can always sway things in their favor. There is really no such thing as a free market. Any system that can be manipulated by those that have more or can make the rules will probably always end up corrupted.

It's amazing to me how someone can be poor and think it's a choice. Unless they're doing absolutely nothing to try and make more money. I can understand rich people saying it because a lot of successful people see their success as it being because they worked hard and took action, and they have survivorship bias. They never attribute their success to also having luck or help from others. If this mentality was true then there would be hardly any poor people. There are tons of poor people who work their asses off trying to better their lives and they have nothing to show for it. We do not live in a meritocracy like we've been led to believe. That someone would "choose" to be poor is a ridiculous concept!

Trauma is subjective, but it still applies to and affects that person.

There are some black millionaires.....therefore all black people can be millionaires, is another ridiculous concept!

How many rich people are alcoholics or drug addicts? Plenty!

Just move to a new place! 🤣 With what money? A bus ticket? Are they supposed to just leave everything they own? Everyone doesn't have family or friends that will take them into their home or even have the resources to do so.

Find another job that pays more? Whew! Some people are clueless with how the economy actually works for the majority of people, huh?

Imagine being so rich that you could give 50 family members $1b each and it STILL wouldn't put a dent in your bank account, while the majority of people have to worry about paying a $50-$100 bill every month etc, and they are one month away from starving or being homeless. There is something severely wrong with a system like that.

As to Kate coming from a small village...what does that have to do with anything? Are they all rich in her small village? Did their tough mentality make them wealthy monetarily? Why did she leave where she's from if all you need is a tough mentality? There are tons of outside factors that a lot of people don't take into account.

8:39 this is fascinating to watch unfolding on screen. I’m not American…but I am aware of the allure of the “American dream” and how it seeks to make the individual to separate themselves from the commune.

The irony is, those with the capacity to overcome, co-opt into the wealth class and wash off the community they escaped from. Irony being…often these individuals are the only ones who have a proximity to assist more people out of poverty (because govt and corporate actively will not). Frankly, I am not oblivious to how impossible an obligation it can be to lift up whole communities (or even sections of)…all the while paying taxes to a government that subverts those same taxes to stifling your individual efforts.

This precise phenomena, is why l feel the movie In Time (Justin Timberlake) should be prescribed viewing (particularly for wealthy folk).

snippet.textDisplay: I’m housed, and unfortunately my blessings have yet to present themselves. I want nothing more than to work and be successful. I had my first kid, he unfortunately was born 3 months early, which caused him to be in the hospital. I was unable to work once he came home, because he wasn’t able to be around other small children, so I had to rely on his father. During that time, my vehicle went out. Since then, it’s been downhill, and I’ve literally been stuck in the house. I’ve had opportunities where cars were offered. The first person went dark. My cousins car she gave me, it needed a timing belt, we found that out after. I’m extremely hard-working, and this is the longest I’ve been without a job. This is the longest I have not been able to take care of myself. And this is definitely not a choice! And I do not have a victim mentality! I’m doing all I can. While all I’m literally trying to do is get a car, and I will be able to takeoff. It just keeps slipping out of my hands. Some of us do what we can, but we do not have the same opportunities as everybody else. I’ve applied for everything I could, but with me not having a job, i’m not applicable. And with my child’s father having 2, and we’re living with him, I’m definitely not applicable. Even though he’s working two jobs, I am absolutely not seeing any of that money, I am still struggling every month, trying to figure out how to get food in the house, trying to figure out how to keep utilities on, doing what I can, with nothing. And yet I’m still trying. That is definitely not a victim mentality! All I wanna do is save work, save, and go tf hooommmmeeeee! I just need some help, that’s all some of us need!

snippet.textDisplay: SOMETHING NO ONE TALKS ABOUT: Many veterans living on the streets often feel uncomfortable with the idea of having a roof over their heads because they don’t want to deal with the rules that come with it. The situation for many people experiencing homelessness is not as black-and-white as it may seem. While some veterans certainly desire housing, their circumstances are quite complex. The construction of more mental health facilities would be beneficial, and it could serve as a pathway to gradually transition them into stable housing. However, many veterans currently on the streets will express a preference for living outdoors rather than in conventional housing situations. This is why I wish there were designated areas around the country where they could live in tents—not in urban settings but within their own communities, allowing them to reside outdoors safely.

snippet.textDisplay:
It’s true tho. These camps are smelly, ugly, and often times dangerous. 

They scare away locals, pedestrians, tourists, and potential customers that might have gone to businesses nearby. It affects people and profit. 

Fix the issue, and more tourists come, and then perhaps spend money. More locals spend money at those businesses. Then the city also looks and feels and smells beautiful (and safe). Property values go up once again. 

It’s a win win win across the board. Doing something is better than doing nothing. It’s in the best interest of everyone, that something is done. For people and for profit. Otherwise an exodus of people and businesses will begin - and in California, it has already begun.

Sincerely…someone who is currently homeless and unemployed in Abbotsford British Columbia.

snippet.textDisplay:
Russian Slavery: Slavery as the status of "kholop" was effectively abolished in Russia in the 1720s by Peter the Great, though serfdom—a system that essentially enslaved peasants to landowning nobles— persisted for much longer. I am sorry, but I feel that it is a choice.  Don't just do what you believe your best is.  Do what is required-- even if it's more than you believe your "best" is.  Elevate yourself.  If I was living paycheck to paycheck-- I would get a second job.  I will do whatever it takes to succeed.

In undergrad, I worked 3 jobs (pharmacy, restaurant, bouncer), so that I could pay my way through without loans and save my GI Bill for my doctorate .  I was on my Universities Powerlifting team.  I graduated with a 3.55.  I didn't get help. I worked 48ish hours a week between the 3. Scheduled all my classes T/Th full-time, and I worked hard.  Listened to recorded lectures while bouncing, driving, and at the gym.  It wasn't easy.  It was so hard.  But I did what I HAD to do to succeed.  I am a big black dude in Texas. It can be done.

snippet.textDisplay:
So the problem is that free will doesn't exist. Or rather people behave in entirely expected ways. If you take 1000 people, and you include some basic information such as their livelihood, race, gender, education, etc...

You can make certain prediction about the people's future that are almost always correct. Such as the number of smokers, alcoholics, other drug users in 2021 based on the addiction of their parents. The number of teen pregnancies based on whether the school in question practices full abstinence sex education, etc...

You can simply predict a future with enormous accuracy based on very few data points and large enough sample size. This proves that humans behave in very expected way if thrust into certain environment. Things like "free will" are just convenient scapegoats when it comes to solving these problems. They don't explain anything, they just give you a peace of mind by allowing you to pretend that you have more control over your life than you actually have.

The upward mobility is incredibly bad nowadays for countries such as US. Simply because it's expensive to be poor. Poor people pay for mistakes that everybody does in a way that other people don't. Imagine an anti-abortion family. If a poor girl gets pregnant, then it's an enormous change of lifestyle. She must immediately start to work, or have to depend on other people. While if a rich girl gets pregnant, her family can entirely absorb the cost no matter what the girl chooses to do. Whether continue to go to school, or work, or take a break from responsibility, it doesn't matter. Same things with healthcare. Poor people might not be able to even afford basic living if they have health insurance. Therefore any little accident can cost them basically everything (que horror stories of calling an ambulance in US). While rich people can absorb the cost no matter what they do. Same with work, education, the quality of life, problems with cops, etc...

Poor people simply don't have the safety net that rich people intrinsically poses, therefore they pay for any on the hurdle dearly. While rich people don't have to deal with those hurdles, or spend money for them to go away..

snippet.textDisplay:
The working conditions for laborers under capitalism are often seen as inferior to the ideals of genuine socialism as proposed by thinkers like Marx, Engels, Lenin, and Bordiga for several reasons:

Exploitation of Labor: Under capitalism, the profit motive drives businesses to minimize costs, often at the expense of workers. Labor is viewed as a commodity, leading to exploitation where workers are paid less than the value they produce. In contrast, socialism aims to eliminate this exploitation by ensuring that workers receive a fair share of the wealth they generate.

Job Insecurity: Capitalism can create volatile job markets, where workers face layoffs and unstable employment. Genuine socialism seeks to provide job security through collective ownership and planning, aiming for full employment and stability.

Lack of Worker Control: In capitalist systems, decisions are often made by a small group of owners or shareholders, leading to a disconnect between labor and management. Socialist models advocate for workers' control over production, enabling them to have a say in their working conditions and organizational practices.

Poor Working Conditions: Profit-driven motives can lead to inadequate safety standards and poor working environments. Socialist principles emphasize the importance of humane working conditions, prioritizing the well-being of workers over profit margins.

Inequality and Class Struggle: Capitalism inherently produces inequality, with a small elite accumulating wealth while the majority struggle to make ends meet. Socialism aims to dismantle class structures and promote equitable distribution of resources, thereby improving the overall quality of life for laborers.

Alienation: Workers in capitalist societies often experience alienation, feeling disconnected from the products of their labor and from their coworkers. Socialist ideology promotes a more collaborative and meaningful work environment, fostering a sense of community and shared purpose.

Social Safety Nets: While capitalist societies may have some social safety nets, these can be inadequate and unevenly distributed. Socialism envisions comprehensive social welfare systems that ensure basic needs—such as healthcare, education, and housing—are met for all, contributing to improved living and working conditions.

you cant "give money to make housing cheaper". Housing would get more expensive (look at any country in recent years that has done those "first time home buyer aid" stuff). 
The only way to make housing cheaper is deregulation, lower rates, encouraging building. If there would be more supply, prices would go down, and also real estate would become less attractive as an investment if the projected price change was negative for the upcoming years, which would also drive the demand down
